feedback_for_solver: The issue is not a local proof gap: the lemma itself is false. For d=r=1 and n=2B+13, any hypothetical C(X,q) with X-support in [-B,B] would force an impossible Laurent-polynomial identity after clearing denominators. You should replace this lemma with a weaker statement (for example allowing support or certificate complexity to grow with n, or allowing a rational-function certificate rather than a uniformly bounded Laurent polynomial one).
reason: The submitted proof is empty, and the supplied counterexample family can be made rigorous. Fix d=r=1 and let B be any proposed uniform X-support bound. Take n=2B+13, which is admissible since n is odd. If C(X,q)=∑_{j=-B}^B c_j(q)X^j satisfied the telescoping identities for k=1,...,n-1, then with X=q^k those identities become 1 = C(X,q) - R(X,q) C(qX,q), where R(X,q)=q^{-1}X^{-1}(1-q^4X^3)(1-qX^2)^3(1-qX)/((1-qX^3)(1+qX)). After clearing denominators, F(X,q):=qX(1-qX^3)(1+qX)C(X,q) - (1-q^4X^3)(1-qX^2)^3(1-qX)C(qX,q) - qX(1-qX^3)(1+qX) is a Laurent polynomial in X with exponents contained in [-B,B+10], hence with at most 2B+11 X-monomials. But F(q^k,q)=0 for k=1,...,n-1=2B+12. Since the q^k are distinct over Q(q), the resulting Vandermonde system forces F(X,q)≡0. Now compare highest X-degree terms: if m is the largest exponent with c_m(q)≠0, then the second term contributes a nonzero X^{m+10} term q^{m+8}c_m(q)X^{m+10}, while the first term has X-degree at most m+5 and the final term has degree at most 5. So F cannot vanish identically. Contradiction. Therefore no such uniformly bounded-support certificate exists; the lemma statement is false.
